What the estimate means

Source: vignettes/estimate.Rmd
estimate.Rmd

You want to know what the nested number means and how far to trust it. This page runs no code. It says why a tuned model’s own score cannot be trusted, which quantity the nested number describes, and how to read its standard error. It also covers fold disagreement and when nesting is worth its cost. The worked example is vignette("nested-cv").

The case for nesting

When you tune with cross-validation, you try several settings, the candidates, and keep the one with the best score. Scores are noisy, and the best of several noisy numbers tends to look better than it is. So the winner’s score overstates what the model will do on new data, by an amount nothing in the output reveals.

At a small sample size the noise is large, so the winner’s score may not even look better than an honest one. Distrust it for how it was chosen, whether it came out high or low.

Nested cross-validation scores the whole tuning procedure, meaning every step you run on the data: resample, tune, pick a setting, fit. Nesting puts that procedure inside a second, outer resampling loop. Each outer fold tunes from scratch on its own analysis rows, fits the chosen setting there, and scores that fit once on assessment rows the tuning never saw.

The number collect_metrics() reports describes the whole tune-and-fit procedure: resample, tune, select, fit. That is the number to report. The model fitted at the end for deployment is a separate object, and it has no performance number of its own. Everything computable from its training data was used up in selecting and fitting it.

The quantity estimated

Take the four steps, resample, tune, select, fit, as one procedure. The number collect_metrics() reports is that procedure’s error when run on each fold’s training rows and scored on fresh data. Bayle et al. (2026) call that the k-fold test error of the procedure.

Four things it is not.

  • It is not the error of the deployed model, which is built afterwards on all the rows and estimated by nothing here.
  • It is not a verdict on that model’s parameter values.
  • It does not say what a larger or a different training set would give, since it ran on this one alone.
  • It is not that error averaged over every training set you might have drawn, which would describe the method rather than this data. Luo and Barber (2026) prove that any assumption-free test of that method-level quantity needs a dataset many times larger than the training set. So this package offers no such test.

A slight pessimism

The number tends to look a little worse than the procedure deserves. Every outer fold trains on its analysis rows only, so every model scored is built on less data than the model you finally deploy. Less data usually means worse predictions. Varma and Simon (2006) separate this training-size effect, which can go either way, from the selection effect, which is always optimistic.

Varma and Simon (2006) ran nested cross-validation on null data with 40 samples, where the true error is 50.0%, and got 54.2%. They attribute the 4.2-point overshoot to training on 39 rows rather than 40. Wilimitis and Walsh (2023) compared methods on 41,121 hospital visits against a held-out benchmark. Nested cross-validation was among the most pessimistic, by roughly 1 to 2% of AUROC and 5 to 9% of AUPR. The same study reports one cell where the nested estimate came out optimistic instead.

The gap is a property of the estimator, not a prediction about any one run. It is never a licence to adjust the reported figure upward.

The standard error

std_err is the standard error of the mean across the outer folds. It is the standard deviation of the fold scores divided by the square root of their number. It is not the fold-to-fold spread, which is larger by that factor. collect_metrics(res, summarize = FALSE) gives the per-fold scores. It is also not a confidence interval. This package ships no inference on the nested estimate.

Comparing two workflows

Suppose you run the loop on two workflows and one comes back lower. Nothing in the output says whether the difference is real, because there is no valid interval to subtract. Bayle et al. (2026) give a sharper reason. A cross-validation interval for one procedure is valid when that procedure is stable. Stable means that changing one training row shifts its errors by little, compared with how spread out those errors are. Two procedures can each be stable while their difference is not, and the difference is what the interval would have to cover. That difference is least stable when the two procedures are similar. A gap between two nested estimates is a reason to look closer, never a result.

The same holds for a set of workflows run through one design with nested_workflow_map(). Choosing the workflow with the best estimate is itself a selection, made on the same scores, and no outer loop scored that choice. So the package offers no ranking or best-workflow function for the set.

Disagreement between folds

When the folds split over a parameter, the data does not pick its value clearly. The estimate is fine, since it already averages over this variability. What suffers is any story about the selected parameters being the right ones.

As two candidates’ predictions converge, which one wins a given fold becomes close to a coin flip (Bayle et al., 2026).

The cost of nesting

Whether nesting pays depends on how much room the selection step had to overfit. Tibshirani and Tibshirani (2009) measured that room on pure noise, where the true error rate is 0.5. With 400 observations and 100 features, the tuned score was under 3 points too good. With 40 observations and 1000 features, the best tuned score of nearest shrunken centroids read 0.384, which is 11.6 points below the true 0.5. Even there the learner mattered: an SVM was 2.5 points too good and a tree only 0.2. In short, the bias is largest with wide data, a big grid, and a preprocessing step the loop has to redo. That paper’s remedy is a correction, not nesting.

Nesting removes little when the data is tall and the search is small. Wilimitis and Walsh (2023) ran that case, 41,121 visits and a modest grid. Nesting bought nothing but the pessimism above, at a cost that grew quadratically in the fold count. Their advice, and this package’s: nest when there are many features for the sample size and the search is wide, if you can afford the compute.

Small data is not safe without nesting. Vabalas et al. (2019) simulated pure noise, where the honest accuracy is 50%. Cross-validation without nesting still reported better than chance at a sample size of 1000. Nested cross-validation stayed at chance at 96.5% of the sample sizes they tried, almost all of them. The bias thins with sample size and does not disappear.

Feature selection inside the workflow

If your pipeline selects features, put that step in the recipe inside the workflow you pass in. The loop here re-estimates the whole workflow inside every fold. Anything done to the data before the call is not re-estimated. No result here can tell that it happened. Vabalas et al. (2019) compared two mistakes: leaving feature selection outside the loop, and leaving parameter tuning outside it. The first was far more damaging.

Bayle, A., Janson, L., & Mackey, L. (2026). The relative instability of model comparison with cross-validation. arXiv:2508.04409.

Vabalas, A., Gowen, E., Poliakoff, E., & Casson, A. J. (2019). Machine learning algorithm validation with a limited sample size. PLoS ONE, 14(11), e0224365.

Varma, S., & Simon, R. (2006). Bias in error estimation when using cross-validation for model selection. BMC Bioinformatics, 7, 91.
